newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Fresh Brazzaville mediation after heavy shelling.
newsitem.headline: Fresh Brazzaville mediation after heavy shelling.

text.p: Brazzaville's mayor, Bernard Kolelas, is trying to persuade the Congo Republic's former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso to accept a nine-point peace plan to end a bloody month-long showdown in the capital.

Kolelas' spokesman Hellot Mampouya said that President Pascal Lissouba, whose forces have been fighting Sassou supporters for control of the city centre and international airport, had on Tuesday accepted the peace plan as a basis for negotiation.
Speaking during a lull that followed heavy evening exchanges of shellfire on Wednesday, Mampouya told Reuters that Kolelas expected to hold fresh talks with Sassou later on Thursday.
"Lissouba considered the nine points were suitable for discussion and said he accepted them as a basis for talks," he said.

The plan centres on conditions for presidential elections that had been scheduled for July 27 before fighting broke out on June 5. Both parties in the conflict have more or less admitted that date is no longer feasible but the presidential poll has not officially been cancelled.
"It would be absolutely surrealistic to hold elections July 27, unless you're talking about July 27, 1998," one Western diplomat told Reuters.

Mampouya said the bilateral meetings with national mediator Kolelas concerned only the nine-point plan and did not extend to proposals made by Gabonese President Omar Bongo, the international mediator in the conflict.
Bongo is trying to negotiate a ceasefire from Saturday.

U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, a key player in international negotiations led by Bongo, said on Wednesday he would ask the Security Council to endorse an African peacekeeping force for the Congo and for the group's wealthier members to pay for it.

"Since neither side trusts the other, both want a peacekeeping force which could supervise a ceasefire and secure the airport to make sure weapons do not flow into the country," he told Reuters. He was due to meet council members Thursday.
There have been several truces in the showdown, in which indiscriminate shooting and shellfire has killed hundreds of innocent civilians. None has held much longer than 24 hours.

Some witnesses said the shelling on Wednesday evening came from the direction of the presidential palace and was directed both towards Sassou's residence at Mpila and towards Bacongo, which is controlled by Kolelas's supporters.
Kolelas's supporters were in the thick of similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 and early 1994 after disputed parliamentary elections.
Bacongo is home to tens of thousands of displaced persons who have fled other parts of town.

Mampouya was unable to say where Wednesday's shelling came from. "All we know is that morning, noon and night people as a matter of course shell Bacongo and Makelekele where there is a large refugee population -- it's completely incomprehensible."

The current conflict erupted on June 5 when troops loyal to Lissouba surrounded Sassou's residence with the ostensible aim of arresting supporters blamed for a series of killings in the north of the country. The move was part of efforts to disband private militias ahead of the election.
